Chinese Hacker Commands DeepSeek via Telegram to Launch Autonomous Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 says a Chinese-speaking threat actor used DeepSeek through the open-source Hermes Agent framework to launch attacks autonomously. After an initial Telegram instruction, the agent found internet-facing systems and selected public exploits. The researchers recovered no further operator input in the session. Hermes/DeepSeek autonomous AI agent artifact: python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the opsec-failure artifact that exposed this campaign: the Hermes Agent (DeepSeek-driven, 'Yolo' unattended mode) launched a Python stdlib file server on port 8888 out of /home/worker, exposing exploit scripts, API keys and session logs. This surfaces the same autonomous-agent tooling running on your own Linux fleet or on a compromised host being used as a staging box. Rationale: Uses the exact opsec artifact Unit 42 named — 'Hermes Agent exposed the operation by starting python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker'. The http.server module + fixed port 8888 combination is the high-fidelity anchor; the /home/worker CWD / 'worker' account is projected as an enrichment flag. Cross-checked Unit 42 and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientist / developer running 'python -m http.server 8888' to quickly share files on a lab host
  • CI runner or container serving build artifacts over the stdlib http server on 8888
  • Internal documentation preview served with http.server on the conventional 8888 port
  • Ad-hoc troubleshooting of a Jupyter-adjacent workflow where 8888 is the habitual port
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in~ ("jenkins","gitlab-runner","builder") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh") and ProcessCommandLine has "/build/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and shell history around the http.server PID — confirm the CWD and enumerate sibling processes (exploit scripts, curl/wget to FOFA/GitHub, other python agents). Check whether the parent is an interactive shell (benign dev) vs an unattended agent/cron. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the listener, and rotate any API keys/tokens present under the serving directory (Hermes exposed model API keys). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for outbound to FOFA/GitHub raw-content, downloaded public exploit files, and marimo/n8n/langflow scanning cmdlines; sweep the fleet for other :8888 http.server listeners.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and ProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| extend HermesHomeDir = (ProcessCommandLine has "/home/worker" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/home/worker" or AccountName =~ "worker")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, HermesHomeDir
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcess = ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Marimo CVE-2026-39987 pre-auth RCE: marimo notebook process spawning a shell AIExploitation High
Hunts successful exploitation of the Marimo unauthenticated /terminal/ws WebSocket flaw, where an attacker obtains a root PTY shell. Detection fires when the marimo notebook server process spawns an interactive shell or recon/download binary — the direct post-RCE landing that the agent used to run commands on 11 Marimo instances. Rationale: Corroborated via GitHub advisory GHSA-2679-6mx9-h9xc / Resecurity: the /terminal/ws endpoint skips validate_auth() and hands back a root PTY, so a marimo (python) parent spawning sh/bash/curl is the unambiguous RCE landing. Parent keyed on 'marimo' in cmdline/path; alternative web-log angle is a WebSocket upgrade to /terminal/ws. Datadog left empty — auditd parent-process correlation isn't expressible with the documented Datadog linux.auditd fields. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2679-6mx9-h9xc • https://www.resecurity.com/blog/article/marimo-pre-auth-rce-via-unauthenticated-websocket-terminal-cve-2026-39987 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/marimo-rce-flaw-cve-2026-39987.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate notebook code cells that shell out (subprocess/os.system) to run tooling as part of a data pipeline
  • Marimo admin running a terminal deliberately for maintenance
  • Container entrypoint scripts where marimo is the PID 1 wrapper spawning shell helpers on startup
  • CI job that launches marimo and immediately shells to install dependencies
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildProcess in~ ("python","python3") and ChildCmd has "pip install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the child shell's command line and downstream activity (whoami/id showing root, curl/wget of second-stage payloads). Correlate with a web request to /terminal/ws around the same timestamp and check the source IP against the >460-target scanning infrastructure. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the marimo process and shell, and confirm Marimo is upgraded to >=0.23.0 (fixed build). 3) Hunt: pull all commands run via the PTY, look for persistence (cron, systemd, SSH keys), and sweep for other internet-exposed marimo/notebook interfaces still on vulnerable versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "marimo"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","id","whoami","python","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or ActingProcessName =~ "marimo"
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","id","whoami","python","python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcess = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NetScaler CVE-2026-3055 SAML IdP memory overread: high-volume /saml/login scraping AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts exploitation of the Citrix NetScaler SAML IdP memory-overread flaw used to exfiltrate data from three organizations. A single source repeatedly hits the SAML IdP /saml/login endpoint to leak leftover request memory (session tokens/data) — abnormal versus real users who authenticate once. Applies to customer-managed NetScaler ADC/Gateway configured as a SAML IdP. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploitation primitive: Horizon3/watchTowr/Fortinet confirm CVE-2026-3055 is triggered by repeated requests to the SAML IdP '/saml/login' endpoint (NSC_TASS) to over-read appliance memory, and the article ties this to data exfil from three orgs. A single source hammering /saml/login 100+ times per 10m is the differentiator from legitimate single-shot SAML logins. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty — NetScaler appliance web telemetry lands in Sentinel CEF and web-proxy datamodels, not endpoint EDR; Sigma skipped because this is a volumetric/threshold detection. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-3055/ • https://watchtowr.com/resources/rapid-reaction-to-cve-2026-3055/ • https://threat-modeling.com/citrix-netscaler-saml-idp-cve-2026-3055/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A busy legitimate SAML IdP fronting many apps where a NAT/egress gateway concentrates hundreds of real logins behind one SourceIP
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring repeatedly probing the /saml/login health path
  • Load-testing or SSO integration testing hammering the IdP endpoint
  • A misconfigured SP retry loop re-requesting /saml/login
Suppression filter
| where DistinctUA <= 2 and SourceIP !in ("<corporate_nat_egress_ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: profile the top SourceIP — is it a corporate NAT egress (many real users) or a single external/hosting-provider IP with one user-agent and no successful auth follow-through? Inspect response sizes/status for the over-read pattern. 2) Contain: block the source at the NetScaler/WAF, and verify the appliance is on the fixed build (14.1-66.59 / 13.1-62.23 or later); if unpatched and configured as SAML IdP, treat leaked session material as compromised and rotate. 3) Hunt: correlate the SourceIP against inbound access to Langflow/n8n/marimo scanning, and review authenticated sessions from tokens that may have been leaked from appliance memory.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC")
| where RequestURL has "/saml/login"
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctUA = dcount(RequestClientApplication), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleURLs = make_set(RequestURL, 5) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Requests > 100    // 100+ /saml/login hits from one source in 10m = memory scraping, not a real login
| order by Requests desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/saml/login*") by Web.src Web.dest _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 100 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Network Anomaly Detection in KATA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-31 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An analysis of how Network Anomaly Detection (NAD) rules work within Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack, using Kerberoasting and DNS tunneling attacks as examples.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1558 T1558.003
Domainstestinglab.ru crust.testinglab.ru
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS tunneling: host issuing many long unique subdomain queries under one parent domain · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Kerberoasting: single account/host requesting TGS tickets for many unique non-system SPNs
Kerberoasting: single account/host requesting TGS tickets for many unique non-system SPNs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact anomaly the KATA NAD 'Signs of a Kerberoasting attack' rule targets: one client account (cname) from one source IP receiving successful Kerberos TGS responses for N or more distinct service (non-machine) SPNs inside a short window. System/computer-account SPNs are excluded because they carry uncrackable auto-generated passwords, mirroring the article's excl logic. Fan-out volume, not encryption type, is the signal. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact NAD logic — KRB_TGS_REP fan-out (dcount of non-'$' ServiceName per requesting cname/source IP) with system SPNs excluded and a count_spns threshold, rather than RC4 signature. MITRE DET0157 independently describes the same 'one account, many distinct SPNs, short window' pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0157/ • https://securelist.com/tr/network-anomaly-detection-in-kata/120892/
ATT&CKT1558.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/BloodHound collectors) enumerating SPNs across the domain
  • SCCM/MECM or monitoring service accounts that legitimately touch many services at startup
  • A privileged admin workstation opening many Kerberos-authenticated apps (SQL, CIFS, HTTP) in a burst after logon
  • Backup/inventory tooling that iterates service accounts
  • Login storms after a DC reboot causing batched ticket requests
Suppression filter
| where TargetUserName !in~ ("svc-scanner","svc-bloodhound","svc-sccm") and IpAddress !in ("10.0.0.0/8-scanner-subnet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on TargetUserName + IpAddress; resolve the source host and confirm whether the account/host normally requests these SPNs. Check if requests came from a workstation vs a server and whether the targeted accounts are high-value (SQL/admin service accounts). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable/force-reset the requesting account and any targeted service-account passwords (assume offline crack in progress), and isolate the source host. 3) Hunt: search for the same source IP performing LDAP SPN enumeration prior to the burst, subsequent logons using the targeted service accounts, and Rubeus/Impacket GetUserSPNs command-line artifacts on the source host.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4769
| where Status == "0x0"                       // successful TGS-REP only (article: KRB_TGS_REP)
| where ServiceName !endswith "$"             // exclude machine/computer-account SPNs (auto-generated strong passwords)
| where ServiceName !in~ ("krbtgt")
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$" and TargetUserName !in~ ("","-")
| summarize UniqueSPNs = dcount(ServiceName), TargetedSPNs = make_set(ServiceName, 25), TGSRequests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by TargetUserName, IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where UniqueSPNs >= 10           // count_spns threshold: single account pulling >=10 distinct service SPNs in 10m
| order by UniqueSPNs desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4769 -@TargetUserName:*$
ENDPOINT
`wineventlog_security` EventCode=4769 Service_Name!="*$" Service_Name!="krbtgt" Account_Name!="*$" Failure_Code="0x0"
| eval win=bin(_time, span=10m)
| stats dc(Service_Name) AS unique_spns values(Service_Name) AS targeted_spns count AS tgs_requests min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime by Account_Name, Client_Address, win
| where unique_spns >= 10
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - unique_spns
DNS tunneling: host issuing many long unique subdomain queries under one parent domain AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the KATA 'Data tunneling in DNS traffic' anomaly: a single host emitting a high volume of unique, abnormally long subdomain labels under one parent zone (encoded data smuggled in the QNAME). Behaviour-based — thresholds on unique-subdomain count and label length rather than a static domain IOC — so it catches the article's example (e.g. crust.testinglab.ru-style beacons) and unknown tunnels alike. Rationale: Anchors on the article's KATA rule shape — per-source high volume of unique subdomains under a single parent zone, with long QNAMEs carrying encoded data — instead of the disposable lab IOC (testinglab.ru / crust.testinglab.ru is a Kaspersky test zone, not shipped as an IOC). MITRE DET0400 corroborates the long-label (>30 char) + abnormal query-volume-to-single-domain signals; thresholds set at 40-char avg / 50 unique labels. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0400/ • https://securelist.com/tr/network-anomaly-detection-in-kata/120892/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CDN / anti-bot providers (Akamai, Cloudflare, CDN edge tokens) that embed long hashed labels in FQDNs
  • Antivirus/EDR cloud-reputation lookups that hash file/URL data into subdomains (e.g. McAfee, Sophos, Trend)
  • Telemetry/analytics SDKs beaconing device IDs as subdomain labels
  • Email security gateways doing SPF/DKIM/DMARC and RBL lookups in bulk
  • Legitimate DNS-based licensing or software-update check-ins with encoded tokens
Suppression filter
| where Parent !endswith "akamaiedge.net" and Parent !endswith "cloudflare.com" and Parent !endswith "trafficmanager.net" and Parent !endswith "amazonaws.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent zone and the initiating process/host; check domain age/registration and whether the zone is a known CDN/security vendor. Inspect sample QNAMEs for base32/base64/hex encoding and consistent length. 2) Contain: if the zone is unrecognised, sinkhole/block it at the resolver and isolate the source host; capture the process making the queries. 3) Hunt: pivot to other hosts querying the same parent zone, correlate to a non-browser/non-system parent process (powershell/rundll32/python) initiating the DNS, and look for matching TXT/NULL/CNAME record types indicative of a tunnel utility (iodine, dnscat2).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Labels = split(RemoteUrl, ".")
| where array_length(Labels) >= 3
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-1]))
| where Parent !endswith "in-addr.arpa"
| summarize UniqueFqdns = dcount(RemoteUrl), AvgLen = avg(strlen(RemoteUrl)), MaxLen = max(strlen(RemoteUrl)), Conns = count(), Sample = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10)
    by DeviceName, Parent, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where UniqueFqdns >= 50 and AvgLen >= 40    // 50 distinct long labels under one zone in 10m = tunneling shape
| order by UniqueFqdns desc
DnsEvents

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, parent], function=[count(field=DomainName, distinct=true, as=unique_long_subdomains), count(as=total_queries)])
| unique_long_subdomains >= 50

Analysis of XCSSET v40 reveals a macOS malware targeting developers via Xcode. Unit 42 used advanced pattern matching and AI to decode its logic. The post The Xcode Assassin Returns: A Deep Dive Into the Latest XCSSET Version appeared first on Unit 42 .

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] XCSSET v40 build-triggered loader: Xcode build spawning osascript/curl · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · Article-specific behavioural hunt — The Xcode Assassin Returns: A Deep Dive Into the Latest XCSSET Version
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] XCSSET v40 chrome_remote backdoor execution and C2 WebSocket egress · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XCSSET v40 CDP hijack: Google Chrome launched with remote-debugging-port · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
XCSSET v40 CDP hijack: Google Chrome launched with remote-debugging-port AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 Chrome-hijacking module activating the Chrome DevTools Protocol by relaunching the legitimate Google Chrome binary with --remote-debugging-port (and, post-Chrome-136, a non-default --user-data-dir) so the dropped chrome_remote binary can attach to the browser engine. Article-specific because it targets the exact CDP-enablement command line the wrapper uses on the real Chrome binary, not headless automation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CDP-enablement behaviour (legitimate 'Google Chrome' binary + --remote-debugging-port, with --user-data-dir surfaced because Chrome 136+ ignores the switch on the default profile). Cross-checked against MITRE S0658 and vendor write-ups confirming the CDP module. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-xcsset-macos-malware-variant-hijacks-cryptocurrency-transactions/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/new-macos-xcsset-variant-targets.html
ATT&CKT1185 T1539 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright test suites that launch Chrome with a debugging port
  • chromedriver-driven CI/automation on developer laptops
  • Manual QA using `--remote-debugging-port` for front-end debugging
  • VS Code / JS debugger 'attach to Chrome' launch configs
  • Lighthouse / performance-profiling tooling launching Chrome with CDP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chromedriver","node","python","python3","Code Helper") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "selenium"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the launching parent — automation binaries (chromedriver/node/python) are benign; a shell, osascript, or unknown wrapper parenting real 'Google Chrome' with a debugging port is suspicious. Check for a chrome_remote binary or a 'boot' process on the same host in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Chrome + chrome_remote processes, and force-revoke/rotate browser session cookies and any SSO tokens (CDP theft is invisible to the user). 3) Hunt: pivot to all Xcode projects on the host for injected loader scripts, look for the C2 URI paths (/s/, /d/, /l, /u) in proxy logs, and check other developer endpoints that cloned the same repo.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "Google Chrome"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chromedriver","node","python","python3")
| extend UsesCustomProfile = iff(ProcessCommandLine has "--user-data-dir", "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, UsesCustomProfile, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "Google Chrome"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ActingProcessName !has "chromedriver" and ActingProcessName !has "node" and ActingProcessName !has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 chrome_remote backdoor execution and C2 WebSocket egress AICommand & Control High
Hunts the dropped chrome_remote Mach-O binary that XCSSET v40 uses to attach to the opened CDP port and open a persistent WebSocket to the rotating C2 for real-time JavaScript injection and cookie exfiltration. High fidelity because chrome_remote is a unique, article-named binary that should never exist on a clean macOS host. Rationale: Pivots on the article's uniquely named chrome_remote binary (the CDP-attach/WebSocket-C2 component) — a name absent from any legitimate macOS install, giving a low-FP, high-confidence signal. Corroborated by MITRE S0658 and vendor reporting describing the CDP cookie-theft backdoor. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-xcsset-macos-malware-variant-hijacks-cryptocurrency-transactions/
ATT&CKT1185 T1071.001 T1539 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely rare — no legitimate macOS software ships a binary named chrome_remote
  • A developer's own project artifact coincidentally named chrome_remote (check code-signing/notarization and path)
  • Security researcher detonating XCSSET samples in a lab
  • An unrelated 'Chrome Remote Desktop' component (verify full path/signature — the real one is 'chrome-remote-desktop', not 'chrome_remote')
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the chrome_remote path and SHA256, verify it is unsigned/un-notarized and dropped outside a normal app bundle; confirm whether it made outbound connections and to which host. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, terminate chrome_remote and its parent Chrome, block the resolved C2 IP/domain at the proxy, and invalidate all browser sessions and OAuth tokens for the user. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same SHA256, for Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC1), and for infected Xcode projects/loader scripts that would re-drop the binary on the next build.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "chrome_remote" or FolderPath endswith "/chrome_remote"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "chrome_remote"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: XCSSET v40 chrome_remote Backdoor Binary Execution
id: 3d71b0a6-4c9e-4f2b-8d6a-9e1f2a7c5b40
description: Detects execution of the chrome_remote Mach-O binary dropped by the XCSSET v40 Chrome-hijacking module to attach to the CDP port and open a WebSocket C2 channel.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/xcsset-v40-malware-analysis/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:
  - attack.t1185
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1539
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: macos
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '/chrome_remote'
  selection_name:
    Image|endswith: 'chrome_remote'
  condition: selection or selection_name
level: high
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 event_platform=Mac ImageFileName=/chrome_remote$/i
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="chrome_remote" OR Processes.process="*/chrome_remote*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="chrome_remote" OR Processes.process="*/chrome_remote*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
XCSSET v40 build-triggered loader: Xcode build spawning osascript/curl AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 initial infection that fires only when a developer builds an infected Xcode project locally — the injected loader runs from an Xcode Run-Script build phase and spawns osascript or curl to reach the C2 and stage further modules. Article-specific because it targets the Xcode/xcodebuild build-tree ancestry that is XCSSET's signature delivery vector. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core delivery mechanic — infection triggers when the developer builds the infected Xcode project, with an AppleScript/curl loader establishing C2. Ancestry on xcodebuild/Xcode + osascript/curl is XCSSET-specific and distinct from generic script execution. Cross-checked against MITRE S0658. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/new-macos-xcsset-variant-targets.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CocoaPods / Swift Package Manager or fastlane Run-Script phases that curl dependencies during a build
  • SwiftLint / build scripts using osascript to post notifications or display dialogs
  • In-house build automation that pings a webhook via curl on build completion
  • Crashlytics/Sentry dSYM upload scripts invoking curl from a build phase
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cocoapods","github.com","swiftpm","fastlane","crashlytics","sentry-cli"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the ProcessCommandLine of the osascript/curl child — benign build tooling references known package hosts (cocoapods.org, github.com dependency URLs); XCSSET reaches short single-letter C2 paths (/a, /s/, /d/) and base64 payloads. Inspect the offending Xcode project's build phases for an injected script. 2) Contain: quarantine the project/repo, isolate the endpoint if C2 contact is confirmed, and block the destination host. 3) Hunt: check whether Chrome was subsequently launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC1) or chrome_remote executed (UC2), and identify every other developer who cloned/built the same repo to scope worming across projects.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("osascript","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".xcodeproj",".xcworkspace","DerivedData","Build/Intermediates.noindex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, GrandParent=InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("osascript","curl")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ParentProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".xcodeproj",".xcworkspace","DerivedData")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Xcode Build Phase Spawning osascript or curl (XCSSET v40 Loader)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

AWS Amplify UI Builder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent — CVE-2025-4318 malicious schema injection AIInstallation Medium
Hunts AmplifyUIBuilder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent/ExportComponent CloudTrail events, the exact API path an authenticated principal uses to import a component schema whose property bindings carry arbitrary JavaScript (CVE-2025-4318). The injected expression re-executes during every codegen/render/build, so the create/update call is the persistence-planting event to surface and attribute to a principal + source IP. Rationale: Uses the concrete eventSource amplifyuibuilder.amazonaws.com and the CreateComponent/UpdateComponent/ExportComponent API names named in the advisory (and confirmed in the AmplifyUIBuilder API reference) — the exact and only path a malicious component schema is imported through. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-010/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react/CVE-2025-4318/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers building/editing UI Builder components in Amplify Studio during normal front-end development
  • Amplify Studio auto-generating components from a DataStore/GraphQL schema import
  • CI service role programmatically syncing components as part of an IaC/export workflow
  • QA or design teams iterating on forms/views/themes
  • First-time Amplify Studio onboarding generating starter components in bulk
Suppression filter
| where userIdentity.type != "AssumedRole" or requestParameters.name has_any ("eval","constructor","process","require","${")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the userIdentity.arn, sourceIPAddress and componentName; confirm the principal is an expected Amplify developer and the IP/geo matches normal dev activity. Retrieve the component schema (GetComponent) and inspect bindingProperties/collectionProperties for expression-like or JS payloads (e.g. constructor, process, require, backtick/${} expressions). 2) Contain: if the schema contains code, delete/roll back the component, rotate the principal's credentials, and freeze codegen builds that pull it (amplify pull / ampx) until packages are on @aws-amplify/codegen-ui(-react) >= 2.20.4. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CreateComponent/UpdateComponent by that principal, check build-host/CI process telemetry for anomalous node child processes at codegen time, and inventory repos for vulnerable codegen-ui versions <=2.20.2.

CLOUD

| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(eventName) as eventName values(sourceIPAddress) as sourceIPAddress values(awsRegion) as awsRegion values(requestParameters.name) as componentName by userIdentity.arn userIdentity.type

AWS Amplify UI Builder create-component CLI invocation on endpoint/CI host (CVE-2025-4318) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts process executions of the AWS CLI 'amplifyuibuilder create-component/update-component/export-component' commands on developer workstations and CI/build runners — the client-side action that imports a component schema and (for vulnerable <=2.20.2 codegen-ui) triggers arbitrary JavaScript during local codegen/build. Complements the CloudTrail UC by catching the on-host command line and its parent process. Rationale: Anchors on the exact 'create-component' command named in the advisory (plus the update/export variants that share the vulnerable binding path) scoped by the 'amplifyuibuilder' service token, so it fires only on Amplify UI Builder schema imports rather than generic AWS CLI usage. Cross-checked against: • https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2025-010/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Front-end developers legitimately importing/exporting components via aws amplifyuibuilder in local dev
  • CI/CD pipeline steps that scriptaws amplifyuibuilder export-component for codegen
  • Infrastructure-as-code sync jobs recreating components from JSON definitions
  • Amplify migration/backup scripts bulk-exporting components
  • Automated tests that provision throwaway components
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("jenkins-agent.exe","runner.worker.exe","buildkitd.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and any --cli-input-json / --component-to-create payload path; open the referenced schema and inspect property bindings for JS (eval, constructor, require, ${}, backticks). Confirm whether the host's node_modules ships @aws-amplify/codegen-ui(-react) <=2.20.2. 2) Contain: on a confirmed malicious schema, isolate the build host/CI runner, kill child node/codegen processes, and block the build from publishing artifacts; upgrade codegen-ui to >=2.20.4 before re-running. 3) Hunt: correlate to the CloudTrail CreateComponent/UpdateComponent event by the same identity/time, review that principal's other Amplify actions, and sweep all build hosts for the vulnerable package version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "amplifyuibuilder"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("create-component","update-component","export-component")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "amplifyuibuilder"
| where CommandLine has_any ("create-component","update-component","export-component")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised npm Packages: @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts Ship an Obfuscated Remote Access Trojan

Installation of compromised @joyfill/components or @joyfill/layouts 2773 beta packages AIDelivery High
Hunts for npm/yarn/pnpm invocations that install the hijacked @joyfill/components or @joyfill/layouts prerelease versions carrying the 2773 marker. These beta tags must be explicitly requested, so any install command referencing them on a dev or CI host is high-fidelity evidence of the supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Anchors on the exact compromised package names plus the '2773' campaign version marker from the article's IOC table; the beta tags are never installed transitively so an explicit reference is near-certain compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/two-compromised-joyfill-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • SCA/EABT tool re-installing the package to reproduce the finding
  • Developer copy-pasting the IOC version string into a test project to verify remediation
  • Internal threat-hunt replaying the malicious install for validation
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonation","malware-lab"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a developer or CI runner and pull the full command line + user; verify the version tag matches 4.0.0-rc24-2773-beta.4/5/6 or 0.1.2-2773.beta.0/1/2. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove node_modules and the offending version, and pin @joyfill to a release published before 2026-07-28; rotate any credentials present on the machine (browser, Git/GitHub CLI, keychains). 3) Hunt: pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for the C2 IPs and to DeviceFileEvents for modifications of @vscode/deviceid, Discord core, GitHub Desktop main.js and the npm CLI on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

Node.js host callout to Joyfill DEV#POPPER RAT C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the four confirmed Joyfill RAT command-and-control IPs (Socket.IO C2 and /$/boot second-stage host). Because the payload runs in-process under Node.js, any host reaching these IPs after importing the package indicates live RAT activity. Rationale: Uses the four verified C2 IPs from the article's IOC block (166.88.134.62 on 443/80, 23.27.13.43 serving /$/boot, 198.105.127.210, 23.27.202.27); direct IP hits are unambiguous. Projecting InitiatingProcessFileName surfaces the offending node.exe without hard-coding a PID. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/two-compromised-joyfill-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared/bulletproof hosting IP later reassigned to a benign service
  • Threat-intel platform actively probing the C2 IP
  • Security proxy/sandbox detonation reaching the IP during analysis
  • Reverse-DNS or connectivity checks by a monitoring tool
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe) and confirm the host has a compromised @joyfill version in node_modules. 2) Contain: block the four C2 IPs at egress, isolate the host, and kill the node process; treat the workstation as compromised and rotate developer credentials. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for the C2 request paths /$/boot, /u/e, /u/f, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /snv and for blockchain-resolver traffic to api.trongrid.io and bsc-dataseed.binance.org from the same host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js spawning a shell or detached node -e child (Joyfill RAT execution) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for node.exe spawning cmd/PowerShell/script hosts or a detached 'node -e' child, matching the RAT's ss_eval arbitrary-execution verb and the article's detached 'node -e' stage that fetches /$/boot. Pairs a node parent with a suspicious child to turn generic exec into an article-specific signal. Rationale: Grounded in the article's 'spawns a detached node -e child' behaviour and the RAT's ss_eval arbitrary-execution verb; the node.exe→shell / node.exe→node -e parent-child pairing narrows generic interpreter execution to the implant's shape. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build scripts / npm run hooks legitimately invoking node -e for scripting
  • Electron/dev tooling shelling out to cmd.exe for platform tasks
  • Test runners spawning child_process shells
  • CI pipelines using node to orchestrate PowerShell steps
  • Local dev servers spawning cross-platform helpers
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node_modules\\.bin","npm run","jest","webpack","vite","eslint"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — benign build hooks reference project paths; RAT activity references reconnaissance, /$/boot fetches, or credential paths. 2) Contain: if the parent node process traces to a compromised @joyfill import, isolate the host and kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents to the four C2 IPs and check DeviceFileEvents for the Python infostealer staging and dev-tool module tampering on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe"))
     or (FileName =~ "node.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has " -e ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where EventID == 4688

| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or (NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe" and CommandLine has " -e ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joyfill RAT persistence injection into developer tool modules (VS Code / Discord / GitHub Desktop / npm) AIInstallation High
Hunts for node.exe modifying the specific developer-tool JavaScript files the RAT self-reloads through: the @vscode/deviceid module, the Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI. Legitimate updates to these apps are not driven by node.exe, making a node-initiated write to them high-fidelity persistence evidence. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's named persistence targets (@vscode/deviceid, Discord desktop core, GitHub Desktop main.js, global npm CLI) and requires node.exe as the writer, which legitimate app self-updates never are. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hijacked-joyfill-npm-packages-worm-like-rat/
ATT&CKT1554 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running a local npm/VS Code extension build that regenerates deviceid modules
  • Electron app rebuild pipeline rewriting Discord/GitHub Desktop bundles from source
  • Custom internal tooling patching npm CLI via node scripts
  • Antivirus quarantine restore rewriting a .js file
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run build","electron-rebuild","webpack"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the modified JS file against a pristine copy of the app/module; the RAT inserts a self-reloading block referencing require/module bootstrap. 2) Contain: isolate the host, restore the affected modules from clean installers, and remove the compromised @joyfill package; rotate developer credentials. 3) Hunt: search for the Python infostealer archive staging, the C2 IP callouts, and the same node-initiated writes across other developer endpoints (worm-like propagation).

| where FileName endswith ".js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileName endswith ".js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known-malicious Joyfill package bundle hash observed on disk AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on the presence of any of the three confirmed SHA256 hashes of the obfuscated Joyfill RAT distribution bundles on an endpoint. This is an exact-match indicator that removes ambiguity even when package version strings or paths are altered. Rationale: Uses the three exact SHA256 hashes published in the article's IOC block for the obfuscated malicious bundles; hash matches are unambiguous. Falcon FileWritten carries no hash field so falcon_logscale_query is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised
ATT&CKT1027 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst storing the sample in a controlled repo
  • Detection-engineering IOC validation copying the file for testing
  • Backup/EDR quarantine artifact retaining a copy of the bundle
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\Quarantine\\","\\malware-samples\\","\\sandbox\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path is inside a real node_modules/@joyfill tree versus an analyst sandbox. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and remove the compromised package version; rotate developer credentials on the host. 3) Hunt: sweep the estate for the same three hashes and pivot to the C2 IP callouts and dev-tool persistence writes on any host that matches.

Compromised @joyfill package artifacts written under node_modules or lock files AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the filesystem footprint of the hijacked packages landing on disk: the specific dist bundle filenames under node_modules/@joyfill/{components,layouts}, plus lock-file writes by a package manager that would pin the compromised release. Complements the process-based install detection with a filesystem-side pivot that survives shell/CI variations. Rationale: Anchors on the exact dist bundle filenames the article says carry the payload (index.js/index.esm.js/joyfill.min.js for components; index.cjs.js/index.es.js for layouts) under node_modules/@joyfill, giving a filesystem pivot independent of the install command line. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/joyfill-npm-beta-releases-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate install of a clean @joyfill version writing the same dist filenames (join to hash/version to confirm)
  • Routine package-lock.json regeneration during any npm install
  • Monorepo dependency hoisting rewriting node_modules trees
  • yarn/pnpm cache restore on CI recreating node_modules
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "\\.cache\\" or FolderPath has "\\Yarn\\Cache\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the package.json version alongside the dist write and compare against 4.0.0-rc24-2773-beta.4/5/6 or 0.1.2-2773.beta.0/1/2, or hash the dist file against the three known-bad SHA256s. 2) Contain: if the version/hash matches, remove the package, pin to a pre-2026-07-28 release, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot to node.exe C2 callouts and to persistence writes in @vscode/deviceid, Discord, GitHub Desktop, and the npm CLI.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has_any (@"node_modules\@joyfill\components", @"node_modules\@joyfill\layouts", "node_modules/@joyfill/components", "node_modules/@joyfill/layouts")
        and FileName in~ ("index.js","index.esm.js","joyfill.min.js","index.cjs.js","index.es.js","package.json"))
   or (FileName in~ ("package-lock.json","yarn.lock","pnpm-lock.yaml") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has_any (@"node_modules\@joyfill\components", @"node_modules\@joyfill\layouts", "node_modules/@joyfill/components", "node_modules/@joyfill/layouts")
        and TargetFileName in~ ("index.js","index.esm.js","joyfill.min.js","index.cjs.js","index.es.js","package.json"))
   or (TargetFileName in~ ("package-lock.json","yarn.lock","pnpm-lock.yaml") and ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Ruby/Puma Rails web process spawns a shell (post-file-read RCE via forged secret_key_base cookie) · [LLM] Internet-facing hosts running activestorage vulnerable to CVE-2026-66066
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rails web process reads /proc/self/environ or app secrets (Active Storage libvips file-read) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Rails web process reads /proc/self/environ or app secrets (Active Storage libvips file-read) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the core arbitrary-file-read primitive of CVE-2026-66066: a crafted upload drives an unfuzzed libvips loader inside the Ruby/Puma process to read the process environment and Rails secrets (secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc). Because libvips is linked into the app process, the read shows up as the web-app binary opening files it never touches at runtime. Rationale: Anchored on the exact read targets the GHSA names as the payoff (secret_key_base in the process environment, master.key, credentials.yml.enc) and scoped to the Ruby web-app process as the actor — that pairing is the file-read primitive itself, not a generic file-access rule. Confirmed via the advisory plus Ethiack and Flatt write-ups that the impact is disclosure of the process environment. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails • https://www.libvips.org/2022/05/28/What's-new-in-8.13.html
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately reading config/master.key and config/credentials.yml.enc at boot (normal startup — not /proc/self/environ)
  • Backup or DLP agents reading /etc/passwd during scheduled scans
  • APM/observability agents (e.g. Datadog, New Relic) reading /proc/<pid>/environ for metadata enrichment
  • Config-management runs (Ansible/Chef) reading /etc/passwd or .env files
  • Container init scripts sourcing .env files at container start
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("rails server","puma","bootsnap"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the actor is the web-app process (ruby/puma) and the read occurred mid-request (not at process start) — correlate the read timestamp against Active Storage variant/representation requests in the web/access log. 2) Contain: if /proc/self/environ or /etc/passwd was read by the app process, treat secret_key_base and every env-resident credential as exposed — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB creds and S3/GCS/Azure Active Storage keys immediately (invalidates sessions). 3) Hunt: check for follow-on ruby-spawned shells and outbound connections from the host, and search web logs for the uploads that preceded the read (/rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads).
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileAccessed"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/proc/self/environ","/environ","/etc/passwd","/config/master.key","/config/credentials.yml.enc","/.env")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/(ruby|puma|passenger|rails)/i
| TargetFileName=/(\/proc\/self\/environ|\/proc\/\d+\/environ|\/etc\/passwd|\/config\/master\.key|\/config\/credentials\.yml\.enc|\/\.env)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
