Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Watering-hole exploit-script delivery from jshosting[.]me (AnySign4PC drive-by) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exploited AnySign4PC.exe spawning child process or dropping DLL · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Exploit AnySign4PC via Hacked Korean Sites to Install Backdoors Without
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SIGNBT/Gunra payload staging via net.tmp and inet.tmp · [LLM] COPPERHEDGE/SIGNBT C2 config in service-registry blobs + unusual service creation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 / reverse-SSH-tunnel to 176.65.128[.]26 (Operation Double Barrel infra) · [LLM] Injected Microsoft process (SyncHost.exe / svchost.exe) making unexpected outbound connection · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anti-forensic evidence destruction: SDelete / CCleaner + 4-char rename-then-delete · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Watering-hole exploit-script delivery from jshosting[.]me (AnySign4PC drive-by) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint contact with jshosting[.]me, the domain AhnLab/KISA attribute to distribution of the version-specific AnySign4PC exploit scripts in both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains. Because the exploit runs with no download prompt, the DNS/HTTP callout to this domain is often the earliest host-visible signal of the drive-by. Rationale: jshosting[.]me is a hard IOC confirmed by AhnLab as the exploit-script distribution domain shared by both the espionage and Gunra intrusions; a corporate host resolving it is high-fidelity given it is not a legitimate service. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1189 T1608.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox that egresses through the corporate resolver
  • Threat-intel enrichment/crawler tooling actively resolving IOC domains
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the query as it blocks it (verify answer is sinkhole IP)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the callout — a browser process is consistent with the watering-hole drive-by; confirm the user visited a Korean news/healthcare/education site immediately prior. 2) Contain: block jshosting[.]me at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and snapshot AnySign4PC version (flag 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for AnySign4PC.exe spawning children/writing DLLs, injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe, and outbound to 176.65.128[.]26.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "jshosting.me" or RemoteUrl endswith ".jshosting.me"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "jshosting.me"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploited AnySign4PC.exe spawning child process or dropping DLL AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation moment where the buffer-overflow in AnySign4PC.exe (Hancom Secure e-signature client) forces the signed process to spawn a child or write a DLL to disk with no user interaction. A certificate-signing client legitimately never spawns interpreters/LOLBins or drops DLLs, so either behaviour from AnySign4PC.exe is anomalous. Rationale: AnySign4PC.exe is the exact exploited binary named by ENKI/KISA; a signing client spawning children or dropping DLLs is behaviourally impossible in benign use, matching Plainbit's 'generated an error and created a malicious DLL without a download prompt'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.enki.co.kr/en/media-center/blog/joint-cybersecurity-advisory-watering-hole-malware-analysis • https://www.file.net/process/anysign4pc.exe.html
ATT&CKT1203 T1055 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AnySign4PC auto-update spawning its own updater/installer (AnySignUpdate.exe)
  • Crash-handler WerFault.exe launched by AnySign4PC after a benign fault
  • Vendor troubleshooting tool bundled with AnySign4PC launching a helper
  • EDR/AV telemetry stub injected into AnySign4PC being recorded as a child
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("AnySignUpdate.exe","AnySignSetup.exe") and not (FileName =~ "WerFault.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-p")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process command line and any dropped DLL path/hash; a LOLBin (rundll32/regsvr32) child or a DLL written to ProgramData/Temp is a strong true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (backdoor decrypts stages in memory and may be disk-absent), and record AnySign4PC version. 3) Hunt: pivot to svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe injection, net.tmp/inet.tmp artifacts, service-registry blobs, and C2 to 176.65.128[.]26 on the same device.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="ChildProcess", InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256;
let DllDrop = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AnySign4PC.exe"
| where ActionType == "FileCreated" and FileName endswith ".dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="DllDrop", InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256;
ProcSpawn | union DllDrop
| order by Timestamp desc

C2 / reverse-SSH-tunnel to 176.65.128[.]26 (Operation Double Barrel infra) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound connection to 176.65.128[.]26, the reverse-tunnelling address AhnLab confirms was reused across both the state-sponsored SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE chain and the Gunra ransomware chain. Any egress to this fixed IP from a corporate host is a high-confidence compromise indicator. Rationale: 176.65.128[.]26 is a fixed IOC that AhnLab confirms as the reverse-tunnelling address shared across both operations — a rare dual-corroborated hard indicator that warrants direct alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/lazarus-group-exploits-anysign4pc-zero-day-to-target-south-korean-financial-sector-via-drive-by-attacks

  • Firewall logging the connection as denied (check DeviceAction=blocked before escalating)
  • Shared hosting rebind — verify the IP is still attacker-controlled at alert time
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","nmap.exe") and DeviceName !has "scanner"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe or an unsigned binary reaching this IP is an immediate true positive; note the port (SSH/reverse-tunnel often 22/443). 2) Contain: block the IP org-wide, isolate the host, and preserve volatile memory before the loader's self-protection wipes disk artifacts. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internal hosts that contacted the IP, and on each check for Mimikatz/NLBrute, RDP fan-out, and service-registry C2 blobs.

| order by Timestamp desc

Injected Microsoft process (SyncHost.exe / svchost.exe) making unexpected outbound connection AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE post-injection C2 pattern where shellcode is injected into legitimate SyncHost.exe or svchost.exe which then beacons out. SyncHost.exe reaching the public internet is inherently anomalous, and svchost.exe egress to the known C2 is a direct hit — both are the article's named injection targets in the espionage and Gunra chains. Rationale: The article and corroborating AhnLab report name svchost.exe and SyncHost.exe as the specific injection targets; SyncHost.exe public egress is behaviourally rare, and svchost.exe to the named C2 IP scopes the noisy svchost case to a hard indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1055.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SyncHost.exe legitimately syncing UWP/Mail-Calendar app data to Microsoft cloud endpoints (filter *.microsoft.com)
  • svchost.exe Windows Update / telemetry to Microsoft IP ranges (excluded via 20.* and MS domains)
  • Third-party sync client mis-named synchost.exe
  • Proxy/NAT collapsing many hosts behind one svchost egress record
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".microsoft.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".live.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".office.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the remote IP is non-Microsoft; a SyncHost.exe connection to an unfamiliar VPS or the C2 IP is a true positive — pull the parent and any CreateRemoteThread (Sysmon 8) targeting the process. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture memory before the in-memory PE is wiped. 3) Hunt: check the same host for AnySign4PC exploitation, encrypted service-registry C2 blobs, and reverse-tunnel egress to 176.65.128[.]26.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SyncHost.exe" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26")
| where RemoteIP !startswith "20." and RemoteUrl !endswith ".microsoft.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".windowsupdate.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "176.65.128.26") or (tolower(tostring(split(SrcHostname,"\\")[-1])) == "synchost.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SIGNBT/Gunra payload staging via net.tmp and inet.tmp AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or execution of the payload files net.tmp and inet.tmp — filenames AhnLab confirms were reused across both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains, with net.tmp invoked with a GUID-format argument. Detects both the file drop and the rundll32/loader execution referencing these temp payloads. Rationale: net.tmp and inet.tmp are exact malware filenames AhnLab confirms across both operations, with net.tmp carrying a GUID-format argument; matching them in command lines and file drops is high-fidelity and rarely benign. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.011 T1027.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate installer or app that happens to write a temp file literally named net.tmp/inet.tmp (rare; verify parent and path)
  • Network-config tooling logging to a *net.tmp scratch file
  • Backup/AV quarantine renaming a file to net.tmp coincidentally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","svchost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the file hash and the full command line — a GUID argument passed to net.tmp via rundll32/a loader is a strong true positive; the loader may side-load a DLL. 2) Contain: isolate the host and image memory (files may be deleted post-load and restored only at clean shutdown with a different hash). 3) Hunt: correlate with AnySign4PC exploitation, service-registry C2 blobs, and 176.65.128[.]26 egress; the same filenames appearing elsewhere may indicate the Gunra pre-ransomware stage.
let Drops = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="FileCreate", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let Exec = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="Exec", FileName, FolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
Drops | union Exec
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "net.tmp" or CommandLine has "inet.tmp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

COPPERHEDGE/SIGNBT C2 config in service-registry blobs + unusual service creation AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the article's named persistence/C2-storage pattern: backdoors that read command-and-control information from encrypted blobs stored under service-registry entries, paired with unusual service creation. Flags registry value writes to CurrentControlSet\Services by non-installer processes and services whose ImagePath points at ProgramData/Temp/AppData. Rationale: The article and AhnLab explicitly recommend hunting 'encrypted data stored under service-registry entries' and 'unusual service creation'; scoping registry writes to CurrentControlSet\Services by non-installer processes and services running from ProgramData/Temp targets that exact tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1112 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate driver/service installers writing binary config under Services keys via a non-standard installer
  • EDR/AV agents storing encrypted config blobs under their own service key
  • Backup or management agents installed from ProgramData with a service entry
  • GPO/SCCM software deployment creating services from staging paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "setup.exe" and RegistryKey !has "Sense" and RegistryKey !has "WinDefend"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and the service ImagePath — a rundll32/unsigned binary writing a REG_BINARY blob under a Services key, or a service pointing at Temp/ProgramData, is a true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, export the registry blob for offline decryption, and disable the rogue service. 3) Hunt: extract C2 from the decrypted blob and sweep for egress to those IPs plus 176.65.128[.]26, and check for svchost/SyncHost injection on the same host.
let SvcRegBlob = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValueType == "Binary"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="SvcRegBlob", RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let SvcInstall = DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="SvcInstall", RegistryKey=FolderPath, RegistryValueName=FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
SvcRegBlob | union SvcInstall
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceFileName has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, SubjectUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\CurrentControlSet\Services\* OR *\currentcontrolset\services\*) -@Image:(*\services.exe OR *\svchost.exe OR *\msiexec.exe OR *\TrustedInstaller.exe)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate RegObjectName=/\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(services|svchost|msiexec|trustedinstaller)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*" AND Registry.registry_value_type="REG_BINARY" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| where NOT process_name IN ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","System")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*" AND Registry.registry_value_type="REG_BINARY" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| where NOT process_name IN ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","System")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Anti-forensic evidence destruction: SDelete / CCleaner + 4-char rename-then-delete AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's named anti-forensic routine: renaming malicious files to random four-character names before deletion, with additional wiping via SDelete and CCleaner observed by Plainbit. Detects SDelete/CCleaner execution and the rename-to-4-char-name-then-delete file sequence. Rationale: Plainbit specifically observed SDelete and CCleaner used for evidence destruction, and AhnLab documented the rename-to-random-4-char-name-before-delete routine; combining the named tools with the rename/delete file pattern targets this exact anti-forensic tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1485 T1070.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using SDelete legitimately to securely wipe free space or decommission a disk
  • IT running CCleaner as a sanctioned cleanup/maintenance tool
  • Software installers creating short temp filenames that get renamed/deleted normally
  • Backup software renaming files to short hashes during dedup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccleaner.exe","CCUpdate.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files") and AccountName !in~ ("itadmin","backupsvc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check who/what launched the wiper — SDelete/CCleaner run by a non-admin user, a service account, or a process descended from AnySign4PC/svchost is a true positive; correlate rename-to-4-char events on the same host and time window. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (evidence is being destroyed) and preserve any remaining volatile memory and MFT. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host's exploitation, injection, and C2 indicators before artifacts are gone, and check for lateral movement (RDP, NLBrute) to other hosts.
let Wipers = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "sdelete" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","-s","-nobanner"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="WiperExec", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName;
let RenameWipe = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileRenamed"
| where FileName matches regex @"^[A-Za-z0-9]{4}(\.[A-Za-z0-9]{1,4})?$"
| where PreviousFileName endswith ".dll" or PreviousFileName endswith ".tmp" or PreviousFileName endswith ".exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="RenameToRandom", FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName=PreviousFileName;
Wipers | union RenameWipe
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe")
     or (CommandLine has "sdelete" and CommandLine has_any ("-p","-nobanner"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

SilverFox Targets Japanese Manufacturer with 3-Driver BYOVD Chain and ValleyRAT

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 15 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chinese cybercrime group known as Silver Fox has been observed using new drivers as part of bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) attacks targeting a Japanese organization in the industrial manufacturing sector to ultimately deliver ValleyRAT (aka Winos 4.0) for persistent remote access. "In this campaign, the group combines new vulnerable-driver abuse, newly observed abuse of legitimate

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] SilverFox Tencent Cloud / QQ staging download (myqcloud + file.wx2.qq.com) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SilverFox 3-driver BYOVD kernel-driver drop (BootRepair/EnPortv/wsftprm.sys) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — SilverFox Targets Japanese Manufacturer with 3-Driver BYOVD Chain and ValleyRAT
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SilverFox PDFCORE8.dll side-load via ConvertToPDF.exe / PDFDirect.exe · [LLM] SilverFox registry-resident payload storage (HKLM\SOFTWARE\IpDates_sun / HKCU\Console\0) · [LLM] ValleyRAT svchost.exe spawned by PDF side-load host for thread-context injection · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ValleyRAT C2 beacon to 43.128.26.132 on non-standard ports 778/779 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SilverFox PDFCORE8.dll side-load via ConvertToPDF.exe / PDFDirect.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the SilverFox DLL side-loading stage where the malicious PDFCORE8.dll loader (which embeds the three BYOVD drivers) is loaded by the legitimate Zeon-signed hosts ConvertToPDF.exe, PDFDirect.exe, or a renamed MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe. Matches on the exact DLL name and the confirmed SHA-256, so it fires on the ValleyRAT staging loader regardless of the host binary used. Rationale: Uses the exact loader DLL name (PDFCORE8.dll) plus the Cato-published SHA-256; both are unique to this SilverFox ValleyRAT chain, so match fidelity is high. Corroborated against the Cato CTRL source blog. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196347/apt/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer-with-advanced-valleyrat-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party PDF utility that genuinely ships a component named PDFCORE8.dll (verify signer and hash)
  • Security-tool sandbox/detonation of the SilverFox sample generating the same image-load event
  • Threat-intel researcher manually detonating the sample on an analyst workstation
  • Backup/imaging software rehydrating an infected disk image
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the loaded DLL's SHA-256 matches 01ccc662...ed01 and note the host process (ConvertToPDF.exe/PDFDirect.exe/MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe) and its folder path; a load from a user Temp/Downloads or ZIP-extraction path is confirmation. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the host in Defender, kill the host process tree, and quarantine the DLL and the sideloading EXE. 3. HUNT: On the same host pivot to the three driver writes (BootRepair.sys/EnPortv.sys/wsftprm.sys), the HKLM\SOFTWARE\IpDates_sun registry key, and outbound traffic to 43.128.26.132:778-779.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "PDFCORE8.dll"
    or SHA256 =~ "01ccc662c4b5d6ff79ede2e5dd7e508c7e2029fcc13e988e22345b0e5413ed01"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LoadedDll = FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "PDFCORE8.dll"
    or TargetFileSHA256 =~ "01ccc662c4b5d6ff79ede2e5dd7e508c7e2029fcc13e988e22345b0e5413ed01"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256

SilverFox 3-driver BYOVD kernel-driver drop (BootRepair/EnPortv/wsftprm.sys) AIExploitation High
Hunts the write-to-disk of SilverFox's three plug-and-play BYOVD drivers — BootRepair.sys, EnPortv.sys and wsftprm.sys (CVE-2023-52271) — dropped by the PDFCORE8.dll loader to gain kernel access and terminate security processes. These exact driver file names in a driver path are rare and high-fidelity for this campaign. Rationale: The three driver file names are the campaign's core BYOVD payload and wsftprm.sys is confirmed as CVE-2023-52271 by a second source (GitHub PoC / OpenCVE); these specific names in a drop are extremely rare outside this actor, giving near-zero benign overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://github.com/victoni/BYOVD-CVE-2023-52271-POC • https://app.opencve.io/cve/CVE-2023-52271
ATT&CKT1068 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WS_FTP / Warsaw (Topaz Antifraud) banking-security software installing wsftprm.sys on a genuine end-user host
  • Vulnerable-driver research VM where an analyst intentionally drops these drivers
  • EDR/AV signature-testing harness writing sample drivers
  • Backup restore of a machine that previously had the driver
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Ipswitch","Progress","Topaz"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a write by PDFCORE8-hosting ConvertToPDF.exe/PDFDirect.exe or from a user profile path is confirmation, versus a signed WS_FTP/Topaz installer. Check if a matching service was registered under HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate host, block driver load, kill the writer process tree, and if a kernel service loaded, plan a reboot only after acquiring memory. 3. HUNT: Pivot to PDFCORE8.dll side-load, HKLM\SOFTWARE\IpDates_sun and HKCU\Console\0 registry writes, svchost injection, and C2 to 43.128.26.132:778-779 on the host and peers.
DeviceFileEvents

| where FileName in~ ("BootRepair.sys", "EnPortv.sys", "wsftprm.sys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileName in~ ("BootRepair.sys", "EnPortv.sys", "wsftprm.sys")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256

ValleyRAT C2 beacon to 43.128.26.132 on non-standard ports 778/779 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections to the SilverFox/ValleyRAT command-and-control server 43.128.26.132 on the confirmed non-standard ports 778 and 779, which the injected svchost.exe uses to fetch shellcode and beacon. Fixed IP + fixed rare ports make this a clean alerting signal. Rationale: Uses the exact ValleyRAT C2 IP and the two confirmed non-standard ports (778/779) from the Cato blog — a static IOC triple with essentially no benign traffic, ideal for alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196347/apt/silverfox-targets-japanese-manufacturer-with-advanced-valleyrat-campaign.html
ATT&CKT1571 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher or sandbox in the org intentionally connecting to the C2 for analysis
  • The IP being re-provisioned by Tencent Cloud to a benign tenant after takedown (verify current attribution before alerting long-term)
  • Threat-intel platform doing an active-scan/validation probe of the IOC
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the initiating process — svchost.exe or a PDFCORE8-related process beaconing to 43.128.26.132:778/779 is confirmation; capture the process command line and parent. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block the IP at egress/firewall, and kill/suspend the beaconing process (do not reboot before memory capture — shellcode is registry-resident in HKCU\Console\0). 3. HUNT: Sweep all hosts for the same IP/ports, then pivot to the driver drops, PDFCORE8.dll load, IpDates_sun key, and the watchdog scheduled task to find the full foothold.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "43.128.26.132"
| where RemotePort in (778, 779)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "43.128.26.132"
| where DstPortNumber in (778, 779)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction

SilverFox registry-resident payload storage (HKLM\SOFTWARE\IpDates_sun / HKCU\Console\0) AIInstallation High
Detects the fileless persistence/storage step where the SilverFox loader writes its C2 configuration into HKLM\SOFTWARE\IpDates_sun and stages downloaded shellcode as REG_BINARY under HKCU\Console\0. The IpDates_sun key name is unique to this campaign and is a high-fidelity, low-volume registry pivot. Rationale: IpDates_sun is a campaign-unique registry key string from the Cato source; matching on it alone yields near-zero benign hits, making it a rare fileless-storage pivot the C2/network rules would otherwise miss. Falcon left empty: this HKLM\SOFTWARE subkey is not an ASEP/autostart location, so AsepValueUpdate (the only FDR registry event available here) would not capture it. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/
ATT&CKT1112 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated third-party app coincidentally naming a key 'IpDates_sun' (extremely unlikely — verify writing process signature)
  • Malware-analysis detonation replaying the sample in a lab
  • Registry backup/restore tooling rehydrating an infected hive
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the writing process is untrusted (PDFCORE8 loader / renamed MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe) and inspect the value data length — large REG_BINARY under HKCU\Console\0 alongside IpDates_sun indicates staged shellcode. 2. CONTAIN: Isolate host, capture memory (payload is registry-resident), then export and delete both keys and kill the loader/watchdog. 3. HUNT: Because the loader and external watchdog re-create each other, verify BOTH the scheduled task/watchdog batch and the loader are killed; sweep for the drivers, PDFCORE8.dll, and C2 traffic.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "IpDates_sun"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has "IpDates_sun"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

SilverFox Tencent Cloud / QQ staging download (myqcloud + file.wx2.qq.com) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts host contact with the attacker-controlled Tencent Cloud bucket (hrefbfdhfhgre-1422102728.cos.ap-hongkong.myqcloud.com) and QQ delivery redirect (file.wx2.qq.com) used to retrieve the next-stage side-loading components. The unique bucket subdomain token makes this a strong delivery-stage pivot. Rationale: The bucket subdomain token hrefbfdhfhgre-1422102728 is unique to this campaign; scoping DNS/network to it (and excluding legit QQ clients for the shared file.wx2.qq.com host) yields a low-noise delivery pivot the endpoint rules miss. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/
ATT&CKT1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate QQ/TIM messenger clients contacting file.wx2.qq.com for benign file transfer (excluded by process filter)
  • Corporate use of the same Tencent Cloud COS region for benign buckets (the unique subdomain token avoids this)
  • Threat-intel sandbox resolving the IOC domain

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("QQ.exe","TIM.exe","QQPCMgr.exe")

1. TRIAGE: Identify the process that resolved/connected — a non-browser, non-QQ binary reaching the myqcloud bucket is confirmation of the downloader stage; capture the fetched file path. 2. CONTAIN: Block the bucket subdomain at DNS/proxy, isolate the host, and quarantine any ZIP/EXE dropped from the fetch. 3. HUNT: Follow the chain forward — PDFCORE8.dll side-load, the three drivers, IpDates_sun key, and C2 to 43.128.26.132; sweep peers for the same domain.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

ValleyRAT svchost.exe spawned by PDF side-load host for thread-context injection AIInstallation High
Detects the process-injection stage where SilverFox's loader spawns svchost.exe (in a suspended state) as the injection target for ValleyRAT shellcode via thread-context hijacking. Legitimate svchost.exe is only launched by services.exe — an svchost child of ConvertToPDF.exe/PDFDirect.exe/MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe is a strong anomaly. Rationale: Anchors on the hard invariant that svchost.exe is legitimately spawned only by services.exe, then pairs it with the exact SilverFox side-load host binaries — a process-tree pivot distinct from the file/registry/network rules and specific to the ValleyRAT injection step. Cross-checked against: • https://www.catonetworks.com/blog/cato-ctrl-silverfox-evolves/
ATT&CKT1055.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application genuinely named MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe located in the real Edge update path launching a helper (verify folder path is Program Files\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate)
  • Analyst/sandbox detonation of the sample
  • Custom software incorrectly reusing the name svchost.exe for a child helper
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains @"\Program Files\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate\"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Verify the parent binary's folder path and signer — a MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe outside Program Files\Microsoft\EdgeUpdate, or any ConvertToPDF/PDFDirect parent, spawning svchost confirms injection. Capture the svchost command line (a bare svchost with no -k service group is suspicious). 2. CONTAIN: Isolate host, memory-capture the svchost process (ValleyRAT shellcode is in-memory), then kill the loader and svchost. 3. HUNT: Because of the dual watchdog, also terminate the watchdog scheduled task/batch and confirm the loader cannot restart; pivot to drivers, IpDates_sun, and C2 43.128.26.132:778-779.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ConvertToPDF.exe", "PDFDirect.exe", "MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "svchost.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ConvertToPDF.exe", "PDFDirect.exe", "MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-52271")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

title: Scheduled Task Creation with Suspicious Image / Encoded Args
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0d
status: experimental
description: |
    schtasks.exe /create with payload-shaped action — points at
    powershell, cmd, rundll32, encoded-base64, or user-writable paths.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1053.005
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to AI-tool anonymizing proxy code.newcli[.]com (knaithe/KnYuan campaign) · [LLM] Direct egress to Chinese-market LLM APIs (DeepSeek/Qwen) from the estate · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Egress to AI-tool anonymizing proxy code.newcli[.]com (knaithe/KnYuan campaign) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections/DNS to code.newcli[.]com, the third-party proxy the actor used to front Claude Code (/ultra) and Codex (/codex/v1) traffic and reduce traceability. Any estate host resolving or connecting to this domain is either the actor's tooling host or a compromised relay. Rationale: code.newcli[.]com is a hard IOC named in Table 1 as the proxy fronting both Western AI tools; the /ultra and /codex/v1 sub-paths are actor-specific. Very low FP as this is not a mainstream service. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A curious developer manually evaluating the same third-party AI proxy service
  • Security researcher replicating the Unit 42 analysis in a lab
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling auto-resolving IOCs from a feed
  • Sandbox/detonation VM fetching the domain during malware analysis
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process/user on the host that resolved code.newcli[.]com — legitimate AI-coding tools do not route through this proxy. 2) CONTAIN: Block newcli.com at the proxy/firewall and isolate the host if the process is an unsanctioned agent framework (python, node, hermes). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host for egress to api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com, and for langflow_poc.py / fofoapi.py execution to confirm the autonomous-attack tooling.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "newcli.com" or RemoteUrl has_any ("code.newcli.com/ultra","code.newcli.com/codex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "newcli.com" or RequestURL has "code.newcli.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Direct egress to Chinese-market LLM APIs (DeepSeek/Qwen) from the estate AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts direct API calls to api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com, the native endpoints the actor hit directly (bypassing the proxy) for DeepSeek and Qwen/GLM/Kimi/MiniMax reasoning. Non-developer estate hosts reaching these are candidate autonomous-attack operator nodes. Rationale: api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com are the exact native API endpoints in Table 1 the actor used directly. Langflow CVE-2026-33017 unauthenticated RCE exploitation (build_public_tmp) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound exploitation of Langflow's unauthenticated code-execution surface (CVE-2026-33017, CVSS 9.8) against internet-facing Langflow instances the campaign enumerated via FOFA title="Langflow". Targets POST traffic to the Langflow code-validation API and mass-scan patterns from the actor's langflow_poc.py. Rationale: Grounded in the article's Langflow phase: FOFA title="Langflow", langflow_poc.py scanner and CVE-2026-33017 (CVSS 9.8). Endpoint /api/v1/validate/code is Langflow's documented unauthenticated code-execution surface; note in rationale it is derived from Langflow CVE knowledge, not verbatim from the article which did not print the path. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://github.com/oscar-mine/CVE-2026-33017-Exploit
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow users saving/validating custom Python components via the UI
  • Internal QA/regression tests exercising the Langflow API
  • Authenticated automation pipelines building flows programmatically
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) safe-checking the endpoint
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Langflow instance version (1.3.4 was vulnerable per the article) and whether auto_login or a public flow ID is enabled — the exploit only succeeds with those prerequisites. 2) CONTAIN: Put Langflow behind authentication, disable auto_login, and block the scanning source IPs at the WAF. 3) HUNT: Review web logs for the same source IP fingerprint hitting many hosts rapidly (mass FOFA-enumerated scan), and check the Langflow host for post-exploit child processes spawned by the app runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "POST" and csUriStem has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| summarize Hits=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent,10) by Computer, cIP, csUriStem
| where Hits >= 1
| order by Hits desc
