Hermes Agent autonomous attack framework execution (fofoapi.py / FofaMap MCP) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of the actor's autonomous offensive tooling on estate hosts: the Hermes Agent framework and its custom fofoapi.py FOFA-enumeration script / FofaMap-Platinum MCP server driving DeepSeek. Catches the operator node itself rather than the victim. Rationale: fofoapi.py, fofa-cyberspace-search, FofaMap-Platinum-Full-Expert MCP, web-terminal-exploitation and godmode are custom, campaign-unique skill/script names from the Technical Analysis section — extremely low chance of benign collision. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red team or purple team replaying the Hermes Agent tooling in a sanctioned exercise
  • Security researcher analyzing the recovered toolset in a lab
  • Threat-intel analyst naming files after the IOCs during investigation
  • A benign unrelated project coincidentally naming a script 'fofoapi.py' (rare)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is not a sanctioned red-team box; capture the full command line, parent process and user. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, snapshot memory/disk, and pull any Hermes Agent config/session logs and Telegram C2 tokens for IR. 3) HUNT: Enumerate the host's home directory for an exposed file server (the article's OPSEC failure), and pivot on outbound FOFA queries, DeepSeek/Qwen API egress and code.newcli[.]com traffic.

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("fofoapi.py","fofa-cyberspace-search","FofaMap-Platinum","web-terminal-exploitation","godmode")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("fofoapi.py","fofa-cyberspace-search","FofaMap-Platinum","web-terminal-exploitation") or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)hermes[-_ ]?agent"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding-tool anti-attribution / permission-bypass config artifacts AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the actor's tell-tale AI-tool hardening: disabling attribution headers and response storage and forcing auto-approval so the agents run unattended. Detects the specific config keys and CLI flags (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0, disable_response_storage=true, dangerously-skip-permissions, approvalMode yolo) on estate hosts. Rationale: These are verbatim config keys/flags from Table 1 and the Tool Configuration section (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER:0, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC:1, disable_response_storage=true, dangerously-skip-permissions:true, approvalMode:yolo). Medium FP because a careless developer could set some of these; the combination or presence on a non-dev host is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running Claude Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions for a trusted local task
  • CI automation setting approvalMode to a non-interactive value
  • Privacy-conscious user disabling telemetry/response storage
  • AI-tool documentation or tutorial commands copy-pasted into a shell
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ () or isnotempty(DeviceName)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine which AI tool set the flag, the user, and whether the host is a sanctioned developer machine. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, isolate the host and preserve the tool config directories (.claude, codex config, qwen config) plus any 'trusted directory' allowlists. 3) HUNT: Correlate with code.newcli[.]com and DeepSeek/Qwen egress and with Hermes Agent / fofoapi.py execution to distinguish a careless dev from the autonomous-attack operator.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dangerously-skip-permissions","CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","disable_response_storage")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)approvalMode\s*[:=]\s*.?yolo"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dangerously-skip-permissions","CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","disable_response_storage") or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)approvalMode\s*[:=]\s*.?yolo"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AI Coding-Tool Anti-Attribution and Permission-Bypass Configuration
id: 1a5c9e40-73b2-4a6f-8e11-6d2f0b9a3c58
description: Detects AI coding-tool hardening flags/keys (attribution disabled, response storage off, permission checks skipped, yolo auto-approval) used by the knaithe/KnYuan autonomous AI attack campaign.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1070
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'dangerously-skip-permissions'
      - 'CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER'
      - 'CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC'
      - 'disable_response_storage'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:(*dangerously-skip-permissions* OR *CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER* OR *CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC* OR *disable_response_storage*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(dangerously-skip-permissions|CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER|CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC|disable_response_storage|approvalMode.{0,3}yolo)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process IN ("*dangerously-skip-permissions*","*CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER*","*CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC*","*disable_response_storage*","*approvalMode*yolo*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process IN ("*dangerously-skip-permissions*","*CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER*","*CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC*","*disable_response_storage*","*approvalMode*yolo*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Autonomous mass-scan burst: langflow_poc.py multi-threaded FOFA target sweep AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the discovery/scanning phase where the Hermes Agent ran langflow_poc.py against a FOFA-enumerated target file at high concurrency (--scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10). Detects the scanner process and the resulting rapid outbound connection burst characteristic of automated, not human-paced, probing. Rationale: langflow_poc.py, langflow_targets.txt and the --scan-file/--threads 10 flags are the exact command from the Langflow phase; combining the process identity with a public-target fan-out burst (>=10 distinct targets/5m matching the --threads 10 concurrency) separates automated scanning from human pacing. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://github.com/oscar-mine/CVE-2026-33017-Exploit
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned internal vulnerability scanning of Langflow assets by the AppSec team
  • A pentester running the public PoC during an authorized engagement
  • Asset-inventory tooling probing internal Langflow ports (7860)
  • Load testing of a Langflow deployment generating many concurrent connections
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the scanning host is not sanctioned scanning infrastructure and review the command line and target file contents (langflow_targets.txt). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block its outbound scanning, and preserve the target list and PoC binary for scope assessment. 3) HUNT: Enrich the target IPs to find which are your own internet-facing Langflow instances, then check those instances for successful POST /api/v1/validate/code exploitation and post-exploit child processes.
let ScannerHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "langflow_poc.py" or ProcessCommandLine has "langflow_targets.txt" or (ProcessCommandLine has "--scan-file" and ProcessCommandLine has "--threads")
| distinct DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where DeviceId in (ScannerHosts)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and RemotePort in (7860, 80, 443)
| summarize DistinctTargets=dcount(RemoteIP), Conns=count(), Window=max(Timestamp)-min(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctTargets >= 10   // 10 = actor's --threads 10 concurrency against many FOFA targets in a tight window
| order by DistinctTargets desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "langflow_poc.py" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "langflow_targets.txt" or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--scan-file" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--threads")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Langflow Mass-Scan Tool Execution (langflow_poc.py --scan-file --threads)
id: 9e2b4d71-0c86-4a3f-bb54-2f7a1c9d6033
description: Detects execution of the actor's langflow_poc.py scanner against a FOFA target list at high concurrency, the discovery phase of the knaithe/KnYuan autonomous AI attack campaign.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:

  - attack.t1046
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_script:
    CommandLine|contains: 'langflow_poc.py'
  selection_targets:
    CommandLine|contains: 'langflow_targets.txt'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--scan-file'
      - '--threads'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@CommandLine:*langflow_poc.py* OR @CommandLine:*langflow_targets.txt* OR (@CommandLine:*--scan-file* AND @CommandLine:*--threads*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(langflow_poc\.py|langflow_targets\.txt|--scan-file.+--threads)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process IN ("*langflow_poc.py*","*langflow_targets.txt*") OR (Processes.process="*--scan-file*" AND Processes.process="*--threads*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process IN ("*langflow_poc.py*","*langflow_targets.txt*") OR (Processes.process="*--scan-file*" AND Processes.process="*--threads*") by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2026-21858", "CVE-2025-68613", "CVE-2026-3055", "CVE-2026-39987", "CVE-2026-34486", "CVE-2026-33824")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Toy Ghouls’ new toy: the GenieLocker ransomware

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-30 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Kaspersky experts dissect GenieLocker: new custom ransomware variants for Windows, Linux, and ESXi systems. We found this family in attacks by Toy Ghouls, a financially motivated extortion group.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1021.002 T1190 T1204.002 T1486

MD5a50eaaf514f4f84e… f08f476f26b01d14… fd46a80c2f455772… de3cfbb50f66079b… 780c8f4c6f077da4…

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe) execution for internal discovery
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] External-partner VPN logon with valid credentials (trusted-relationship abuse)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Toy Ghouls’ new toy: the GenieLocker ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] socks5.exe / anomalous Windows OpenSSH server for pivot tunneling · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse SSH tunnel and C2 beacon to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GenieLocker Windows ransomware execution via secret-argument hex + --percent/--recursive flags · [LLM] Mimikatz credential dumping via command-line/module signature · [LLM] KeePassXC .kdbx vault access/copy by non-KeePass process · [LLM] GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi via --percent/--recursive flags · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change
GenieLocker Windows ransomware execution via secret-argument hex + --percent/--recursive flags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of the GenieLocker PE encryptor, which requires a long hex 'secret argument' as its first parameter and exposes distinctive --percent/-p and --recursive/-r CLI flags plus a -l/--log path. Anchors on the confirmed Windows sample MD5 and the malware's unique command-line shape. Rationale: Uses the article's confirmed Windows sample MD5 (5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c) and the malware's documented argument table (-p/--percent, -r/--recursive, -l/--log) — the --percent+--recursive combination is a rare, high-fidelity anchor for an encryptor. Cross-checked with gbhackers and mallory.ai malware profiles. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/ • https://mallory.ai/malware/019d2af9-67da-7113-b5e6-2e6c809b97b1
ATT&CKT1486 T1480.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/imaging utility invoked with both --percent (progress) and --recursive flags
  • Custom sysadmin file-processing scripts that mirror those long-flag names
  • Security-team detonation of the sample in a sandbox using the real secret argument
  • File-integrity or compression tools with a --recursive + --log combination
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","veeamagent.exe") and MD5 != "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent process; confirm the first argument is a long hex string and MD5 matches a GenieLocker sample. Check the target path passed as the last argument. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network immediately, kill the process tree, and preserve volatile memory before shutdown to avoid losing per-file keys. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same MD5 and the --percent/--recursive command line across all hosts (mass deployment via PsExec/PAExec is expected), and look for preceding netscan.exe/mimikatz/socks5.exe activity on the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where MD5 == "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "--percent" and CommandLine has "--recursive") or (CommandLine has "--percent" and CommandLine has "--log")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GenieLocker Windows Ransomware Execution (secret-arg + encrypt flags)
id: 7c3a1e42-9f1b-4c67-b0e2-1a4d9b2c8e10
description: Detects GenieLocker PE encryptor via its confirmed MD5 or its distinctive --percent/--recursive/--log command-line flags.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1486
  - attack.t1480.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_hash:
    MD5: '5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c'
  selection_cli:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--percent'
      - '--recursive'
  condition: selection_hash or selection_cli
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate archivers or backup CLIs that coincidentally use --percent and --recursive together
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Hashes:*5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c* OR (@CommandLine:*--percent* AND @CommandLine:*--recursive*) OR (@CommandLine:*--percent* AND @CommandLine:*--log*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| MD5HashData=/^5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c$/i OR (regex("--percent", field=CommandLine) AND regex("--recursive", field=CommandLine)) OR (regex("--percent", field=CommandLine) AND regex("--log", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, MD5HashData], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_hash="5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c" OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--recursive*") OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--log*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_hash="5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c" OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--recursive*") OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--log*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
External-partner VPN logon with valid credentials (trusted-relationship abuse) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the GenieLocker initial-access vector: successful network/RDP logons using valid domain credentials that originate from a public (external partner) IP, consistent with the reported OpenVPN entry from a trusted partner's network. Flags externally-sourced authenticated sessions that precede internal tooling activity. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit initial-access statement (OpenVPN from an external partner network with stolen-but-valid credentials, T1199 trusted relationship). Detects authenticated sessions sourced from public IPs — the observable signature of externally-terminated VPN/RDP access with valid accounts. Confirmed by cybersecuritynews and gbhackers write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1078 T1199
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate partner/vendor remote support sessions over VPN or RDP
  • Remote employees connecting from home ISPs when the VPN gateway forwards the real public source IP
  • Cloud-hosted jump boxes with public NICs authenticating to domain resources
  • Split-tunnel VPN configurations that expose the client's public IP on network logons
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("<approved-partner-vpn-egress-not-applicable>") == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate the RemoteIP and confirm whether it belongs to a sanctioned partner range; verify the account is expected to authenticate externally and whether MFA was satisfied. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable the account, force credential reset, and terminate active sessions at the VPN concentrator. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account across DeviceProcessEvents for netscan.exe/mimikatz/socks5.exe and on DeviceLogonEvents for subsequent RDP/SSH lateral movement to other hosts.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("Network","RemoteInteractive")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hosts=make_set(DeviceName,20), Count=count() by AccountName, RemoteIP, LogonType
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4624
| where LogonType in (3,10)
| where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress !in ("-","::1","127.0.0.1")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(IpAddress))
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Hosts=make_set(Computer,20) by TargetUserName, IpAddress, LogonType
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4624 @LogonType:(3 OR 10) NOT (CIDR(@IpAddress, 10.0.0.0/8) OR CIDR(@IpAddress, 172.16.0.0/12) OR CIDR(@IpAddress, 192.168.0.0/16)) -@TargetUserName:*$
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| LogonType=/^(3|10)$/
| RemoteAddressIP4=*
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| UserName!=/\$$/
| groupBy([UserName, RemoteAddressIP4, LogonType, ComputerName], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" (Authentication.authentication_method="NTLM" OR Authentication.authentication_method="Kerberos" OR nodename=Authentication) by Authentication.src Authentication.user Authentication.dest Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where user!="*$" AND NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | iplocation src | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action="success" (Authentication.authentication_method="NTLM" OR Authentication.authentication_method="Kerberos" OR nodename=Authentication) by Authentication.src Authentication.user Authentication.dest Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where user!="*$" AND NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | iplocation src | sort - lastTime
SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe) execution for internal discovery AIReconnaissance High
Detects the SoftPerfect Network Scanner used by Toy Ghouls for host/network discovery, matching on the netscan.exe image name and, resiliently, on the SoftPerfect vendor/product version metadata so renamed copies are still caught. Rationale: Article names 'SoftPerfect Network Scanner' as the discovery tool. Anchoring on both the netscan.exe image name and the SoftPerfect product/company PE metadata defeats simple renames while staying specific to this campaign's toolset. Corroborated by gbhackers and cybersecuritynews. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned IT teams using SoftPerfect Network Scanner for asset inventory
  • Network engineers troubleshooting connectivity with the same tool
  • MSP/consultant onboarding scans
  • Vulnerability-management pilots evaluating SoftPerfect
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-itasset","svc-netmon")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing account and host are authorized to run network-scanning tools; review the scan's target ranges in the command line/config. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host and disable the account pending review. 3) Hunt: on the same host/account look for Mimikatz command lines, socks5.exe/sshd.exe, and outbound connections to 89.125.66.101 — netscan is typically the discovery step that precedes credential access and lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "netscan.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "netscan.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Network Scanner"
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "SoftPerfect"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\netscan.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mimikatz credential dumping via command-line/module signature AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Mimikatz execution used by Toy Ghouls to dump credentials, anchoring on its signature command modules (sekurlsa::, lsadump::, privilege::debug) and PE metadata rather than LSASS memory access, so renamed binaries are still caught. Rationale: Article states Mimikatz was used to dump credentials. Matching on module strings (sekurlsa::/lsadump::/privilege::debug) and gentilkiwi PE metadata is high-fidelity and deliberately avoids the pre-existing generic LSASS-access rule. Corroborated by cybersecuritynews and gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned red-team/pentest engagements running Mimikatz
  • Security tooling that bundles Mimikatz modules for detection testing
  • EDR/AV signature files containing the module strings scanned into a command line (rare)
  • Purple-team detection-validation exercises
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "redteam" and DeviceName !in~ ("PURPLELAB01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent process; confirm elevation (privilege::debug requires admin) and whether an active red-team engagement is scheduled. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset credentials for every account that had a session on it, and rotate service-account/krbtgt if domain admin material was exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot on the harvested accounts across DeviceLogonEvents for RDP/SSH lateral movement and on KeePassXC .kdbx access on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","lsadump::","privilege::debug","kerberos::","crypto::","mimikatz")
   or FileName =~ "mimikatz.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "mimikatz.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoFileDescription has "mimikatz"
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "gentilkiwi"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","lsadump::","privilege::debug","kerberos::","mimikatz")
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\mimikatz.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

KeePassXC .kdbx vault access/copy by non-KeePass process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects attempts to steal credentials from KeePassXC databases, as reported in the intrusion: a .kdbx file being created/copied or referenced in a command line by any process other than KeePassXC/KeePass (shells, archivers, copy utilities). Rationale: Article states the actors accessed KeePassXC databases on several hosts to extract stored credentials. A .kdbx write/copy by anything other than the KeePass client is a targeted, high-signal credential-store theft indicator (T1555.005). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/
ATT&CKT1555.005 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup agents (Veeam, CrashPlan, OneDrive/Backup) copying profile folders containing .kdbx
  • A user manually copying their own vault to a USB drive or network share
  • File-sync clients (Dropbox/Nextcloud) replicating a .kdbx
  • Migration tooling moving a user profile to a new machine
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeamagent.exe","onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","backup.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Backup\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and destination path — a copy to Temp/Public/network share or an archiver (7z/rar) reading .kdbx is high concern; a backup agent to a backup path is likely benign. 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate the host and force reset of every credential potentially stored in that vault. 3) Hunt: correlate with Mimikatz execution and outbound transfer/staging on the same host, and check whether the .kdbx was subsequently archived or moved toward the C2 IP 89.125.66.101.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("keepassxc.exe","keepass.exe","keepassxc-cli.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !has "keepass"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

socks5.exe / anomalous Windows OpenSSH server for pivot tunneling AIInstallation Medium
Detects the pivot/tunneling toolkit Toy Ghouls installed on compromised Windows hosts — the named socks5.exe proxy binary, an OpenSSH sshd.exe server running on a Windows endpoint, and ssh.exe dynamic-SOCKS (-D) proxying — used to build lateral-movement infrastructure. Rationale: Article lists socks5.exe and OpenSSH among tools installed on compromised hosts for pivoting. socks5.exe is a specific binary name; an sshd.exe server or ssh -D dynamic proxy on Windows endpoints is anomalous tunneling infrastructure (T1572/T1090). Confirmed by gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1021.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Servers where Windows OpenSSH Server (sshd.exe) is a sanctioned, installed role
  • Developers/admins using ssh -D for legitimate SOCKS forwarding
  • Third-party VPN or remote-access software that bundles a socks proxy component
  • Automation/CI agents launching sshd for build tasks
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "sshd.exe" and DeviceName in~ ("LINUXJUMP01","SSHGW01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether OpenSSH Server / SOCKS proxying is an approved service on this host; review the binary path (Temp/Public/user profile = suspicious) and command-line listen ports. 2) Contain: kill the process, block the listening port, and isolate the host if the tooling is unsanctioned. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents from this host to 89.125.66.101 and for inbound connections to the socks/ssh listener from other internal hosts (pivot fan-out).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "socks5.exe"
   or FileName =~ "sshd.exe"
   or (FileName =~ "ssh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-D")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\socks5.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\sshd.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe" and CommandLine has "-D")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: socks5.exe / Anomalous OpenSSH Server on Windows (Toy Ghouls pivot)
id: 5f2b8c91-7a63-4d0e-b1a4-9c3e2d6f8b17
description: Detects socks5.exe proxy, a Windows OpenSSH sshd server, or ssh.exe dynamic-SOCKS proxying used for lateral-movement tunneling.

Reverse SSH tunnel and C2 beacon to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the reverse SSH tunnel Toy Ghouls established for command-and-control: any outbound connection to the confirmed C2 IP 89.125.66.101, and ssh.exe/plink reverse-forwarding (-R) to a public host — the network signature of the C2 channel. Rationale: IP 89.125.66.101 is the article's C2 indicator (corroborated by the Securelist IOC list and mallory.ai). Combined with ssh.exe/plink '-R' reverse-forwarding to public destinations — the exact reverse-SSH-tunnel C2 technique the article describes — this is a high-fidelity C2 detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://mallory.ai/malware/019d2af9-67da-7113-b5e6-2e6c809b97b1
ATT&CKT1572 T1071 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/allowlist scanners or sinkholes deliberately touching the IOC
  • Security researchers detonating samples in a monitored lab
  • Admins using ssh -R for legitimate reverse-forwarding to a sanctioned bastion
  • Netflow re-ingestion causing historical hits after the IOC is already remediated
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threatintel" and DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARELAB01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcessFileName) and account driving the connection to 89.125.66.101; determine direction and byte volume. 2) Contain: block 89.125.66.101 at the perimeter, isolate the beaconing host, and terminate any ssh.exe/plink -R sessions. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to the IP and for socks5.exe/sshd.exe pivot infrastructure, then check for GenieLocker execution (UC1) as encryption often follows C2 setup.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.125.66.101"
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ssh.exe","plink.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-R" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "89.125.66.101"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101

GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi via --percent/--recursive flags AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GenieLocker ELF build used to encrypt Linux servers and ESXi datastores after stopping running VMs. Anchors on the shared encryptor CLI flags (--percent/-p, --recursive/-r, --log/-l) executed on Linux hosts. Rationale: Article documents an ELF GenieLocker build encrypting Linux/ESXi servers after stopping VMs, sharing the same argument set (-p/--percent, -r/--recursive, -l/--log) as the Windows build. Scoping those flags to Linux process telemetry targets the ESXi/Linux impact phase. Cross-platform behaviour confirmed by technadu and gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Linux backup or rsync-style utilities invoked with --percent progress and --recursive together
  • ESXi/admin maintenance scripts that batch-process datastore files with similar flags
  • Media/transcoding jobs using --recursive over a tree with a --log destination
  • Legitimate encryption/compression CLI tools run by admins
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("rsync","tar","borg","restic","duplicity")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the path argument; on ESXi correlate with recent vmsvc power-off / VM shutdown activity and check the binary against GenieLocker ELF hashes. 2) Contain: kill the process, disconnect the host/datastore from the network, and protect backups/snapshots from deletion. 3) Hunt: check SSH access logs for the reverse tunnel and connections to 89.125.66.101, and review other Linux/ESXi hosts reachable over SSH for the same flag pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| where FolderPath startswith "/" or FolderPath has "/tmp/" or FolderPath has "/var/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux" or ActingProcessName startswith "/"
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
     or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("89.125.66.101")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

let BadHashes = dynamic(["a50eaaf514f4f84e61ca2455a8789753", "f08f476f26b01d142ca73923de65fc0c", "fd46a80c2f45577263328984edf7f4dc", "de3cfbb50f66079bfee20a6f64e59433", "780c8f4c6f077da4da96582987920362", "d87d0b01d95acc936b7dc47b8f41937a", "34a7f28e0bb69b0d49bacc88bdf20ac1", "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c", "a8842616c9057d5cf6e1fe1fa8c3c160", "34b8828635f88078735799a3c1ac8e28", "d3e06eb34d8eee7ef92cac3ad0a20ff5", "c68b6862725777651085650db34947fc", "9cd514ff2809ce0b993e3b8649e82a94", "824ca1e906cc073ee5b0f3519df69a8f", "25480dad40152ef3d0c6d38eecc9bd9b", "7dad78584795aa5c160520cc6accf260", "18f61c6d686cffd131c9fd3f3437064b", "9969a8221312dba70dd5cbddf83a146c", "f7b9e36e94163a9a303160945f99267a", "b893eafed0659f70d4ac250f09073723", "d661cf666b9acbab7cfeae1127a261a9", "3a4479b51890373bfc4a011ef41fe376", "58c0dda52b8f069660166d61fd74f911", "9201e35e2993612612919a3c71302cab"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OWAReaper server-side persistence: Owner rights granted to Default/Anonymous on mail folders · [LLM] Successful OWA/Exchange access within 24h of a password reset (post-rotation mailbox access) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OWAReaper C2 / exfiltration to TA488-controlled domains (HTTPS + DNS label tunneling) · [LLM] First-seen OWA/Exchange sign-in from Russian IP space for a user with no RU history · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
OWAReaper server-side persistence: Owner rights granted to Default/Anonymous on mail folders AIInstallation High
Hunts the core OWAReaper persistence mechanism where the implant uses Outlook APIs to grant Owner-level permissions to the Default (or Anonymous) principal on every mail folder, giving any authenticated org user complete mailbox access that survives credential rotation and device re-imaging. Fires on Add/Set-MailboxFolderPermission cmdlets assigning Owner/Editor rights to Default or Anonymous. Rationale: Article states OWAReaper 'grants itself Owner-level permissions to the Default user on every mail folder... grants complete mailbox access to any authenticated user' and that this 'lives on the server-side and requires deliberate removal from the Exchange server.' Granting Owner/Editor to Default/Anonymous is the highest-fidelity, article-specific persistence artifact and is directly logged in Exchange admin audit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-exchange-owa-zero-day-for-long-term-mailbox-access/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/30/cve-2026-42897-microsoft-exchange-email-attack/
ATT&CKT1098.002 T1098
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Calendar-sharing/publishing that sets Default to Reviewer or AvailabilityOnly (not Owner) — excluded by the rights filter
  • Shared/resource mailbox admin delegation scripts intentionally opening a mailbox to Default
  • Mailbox migration or coexistence tooling re-applying folder permissions in bulk
  • Help-desk delegation runbooks granting Editor on a specific folder to a named team member (User is not Default/Anonymous)
Suppression filter
| where not (Parameters has_any ("AvailabilityOnly","LimitedDetails","Reviewer","None") and Parameters !has "Owner" and Parameters !has "Editor")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full Parameters/RawEventData — confirm the User is literally 'Default' or 'Anonymous' and AccessRights includes Owner/Editor; identify the acting principal (UserId/AccountId) and ClientIP, and whether the acting account is itself recently compromised. 2) Contain: run Remove-MailboxFolderPermission to strip Default/Anonymous Owner rights on every folder of the affected mailbox, revoke the acting account's sessions/tokens (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken), and force MFA re-registration. 3) Hunt: enumerate all mailboxes in the org for Default/Anonymous Owner/Editor grants, review the acting IP for connections to asecdns.com/acocdn.com/dnsrecursive.eu/tdndns.com, and check for OWAReaper's localStorage/IndexedDB re-infection on the victim's browser.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Exchange"
| where ActionType in~ ("Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("Owner","Editor","PublishingEditor")
| where Raw has_any ("Default","Anonymous")
| project Timestamp, ActingUser = AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, ActionType, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in~ ("Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")
| where Parameters has_any ("Owner","Editor","PublishingEditor")
| where Parameters has_any ("Default","Anonymous")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, MailboxOwnerUPN, Parameters, ResultStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OWAReaper Mailbox Folder Permission Grant to Default or Anonymous
id: 4d9f1c2e-7a6b-4b2f-9c1a-2e8b6f3a1d54
description: Detects Add/Set-MailboxFolderPermission granting Owner/Editor rights to the Default or Anonymous principal, the server-side persistence used by OWAReaper (TA488/Void Blizzard) that survives credential rotation.
references:
  - https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-hackers-exploit-microsoft-owa.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1098.002
logsource:
  product: m365
  service: exchange
detection:
  selection_cmd:
    Operation:
      - 'Add-MailboxFolderPermission'
      - 'Set-MailboxFolderPermission'
  selection_principal:
    Parameters|contains:
      - 'Default'
      - 'Anonymous'
  selection_rights:
    Parameters|contains:
      - 'Owner'
      - 'Editor'
      - 'PublishingEditor'
  condition: selection_cmd and selection_principal and selection_rights
level: high
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
`summariesonly` | tstats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action=modified AND (All_Changes.command IN ("Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")) by All_Changes.user All_Changes.object All_Changes.command All_Changes.result _raw | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | search _raw="*Owner*" AND (_raw="*Default*" OR _raw="*Anonymous*") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
summariesonly=false | tstats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action=modified AND (All_Changes.command IN ("Add-MailboxFolderPermission","Set-MailboxFolderPermission")) by All_Changes.user All_Changes.object All_Changes.command All_Changes.result _raw | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | search _raw="*Owner*" AND (_raw="*Default*" OR _raw="*Anonymous*") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OWAReaper C2 / exfiltration to TA488-controlled domains (HTTPS + DNS label tunneling) AICommand & Control High
Detects any host resolving or connecting to the four attacker-controlled OWAReaper domains used for HTTPS exfiltration and DNS-label tunneling. High-fidelity IOC match confirmed by multiple second sources; matches parent domain to also catch DNS-tunnel subdomains. Rationale: asecdns.com, acocdn.com, dnsrecursive.eu and tdndns.com are the pre-extracted C2/exfil domains and were independently confirmed by BleepingComputer and betanews; the article states exfil is 'primarily over HTTPS with AES-CTR encrypted URI paths' with fallback to 'DNS label tunneling... of an actor-controlled domain', so both endswith (subdomain-tunnel) and URL matches apply. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-exchange-owa-zero-day-for-long-term-mailbox-access/ • https://betanews.com/article/russian-hackers-owareaper-exchange-backdoor/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/cleaning-out-inboxes-ta488-comes-outlook-another-half-click-exploit
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1572 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanners / sandboxes in the org deliberately resolving these IOCs for enrichment
  • Security researcher workstation reproducing the campaign
  • Passive DNS or DNS-sinkhole appliance logging the domains as it blocks them
  • Typo-squat collisions are unlikely given the specific TLDs but a benign lookalike could theoretically appear
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host, the ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcess (expect a browser process hosting the OWA tab), and whether the query is a bare apex or a long random subdomain label (DNS tunnel). 2) Contain: block all four domains at the resolver/proxy, isolate the host's browser session, and clear OWAReaper's browser localStorage/IndexedDB persistence for the user. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolving browser process for concurrent HTTPS beacons routed through image CDNs (images.weserv.nl, i3.wp.com, slack-imgs.com) toward acocdn.com, and check the user's mailbox for Default/Anonymous Owner folder-permission grants.
